verses.verse:
तूर्याष्टमौ कनिष्ठाभ्याम् वादकाश्छादयन्त्यथ।
विपरीतस्थितेडङ्गुष्ठां छिद्रे रक्षन्ति साधकाः।७५।
verses.text: Then players cover the fourth and the eighth [holes] with the little fingers; and practitioners keep the thumb on the hole placed on the opposite side.

verses.verse:
पूर्वक्रमेण छिद्राणि तर्जन्याद्यंगुलीयकैंः।
प्राच्छादयेदवक्रेण स्वल्प वक्रेण वा क्वचित्।७६।
verses.text: The holes should be covered in the earlier order with the fingers beginning with the index finger, keeping them straight, or sometimes slightly bent.

commentary.text: That is, closing the holes in order from the top with the index and the other fingers according to the earlier rule, in a flute with eight holes close the fourth and the eighth holes with the kaniṣṭhā, that is, the smallest fingers. If, besides the eight, there is a ninth hole from the bottom on the opposite side, close it with the thumb. If, when making the flute, the holes are made with the placement of the fingers in mind, the holes will not all lie in a straight line but will certainly look somewhat crooked; but this brings quick success in practice and does no harm. If, tempted by good looks, the holes are set in a straight line, crookedness will come into the placement of the fingers, and that could stand in the way of success. That is why practitioners today feel hardship on large flutes. It was largely to solve these very difficulties that the late Śrī Pannalal Ghosh ji had his fingers lengthened by surgery. This was certainly a sign of his boundless devotion, but for his followers it became a hard nut to crack.

The solution I have found for this will be scientifically acceptable to all. If a separate hole is made between Dha and Ni for komal Ni, and between Re and Ga for komal Ga, there are three benefits: (1) the distance between the holes becomes smaller; (2) clarity comes easily in rāgas with komal notes; (3) greater success is gained in the action of mīṇḍ (glide). So practitioners are requested to make and practise on a nine-hole flute from the very beginning. This is made clear in the figure ahead. Here figure (7) is for those who like to keep the left hand below. Figure (8) is for those with the opposite preference. We have made this design after checking carefully that it poses no difficulty for the placement of human fingers. Here the hole at the very top is for placing the thumb, so by giving it a place on the edge of the flute it is shown that the thumb too is placed not fully at the back but pressed to the right or the left. If you feel some discomfort, you can make the rows of holes more crooked or straighter, depending on the thickness of the flute. This will make no difference to the notes, because the difference between the notes depends on the distance between the holes and on the size of the holes.

At the start, practitioners should practise on a flute one hasta (cubit) long, measured by their own arm. Then after one year it will be right to practise on one of one and a half hastas, and after two years on a flute of about two hastas. This process will lead the placement of the fingers naturally towards progress. See the length of the flute, according to the tastes of the three stages of life — childhood, youth and maturity — in the ślokas written below.
